99.29% Sync - discovered what the remaining 0.71% is

Searching online I found some other folks stranding on a 99.29% sync percentage, wondering where the remaining 0.71% is to be found.

There's one San Giminiano side mission called 'Don't Get Your Hands Dirty', gently requiring you to not use any weapon to carry out the four assassinations. Since 100% sync was only introduced in Brotherhood, there's no indicator during or after the mission to track if you fullfilled the requirements, since you can finish the mission using weapons. This mission might be one of the seeds that led to the 100% sync mechanic in the following titles.

So for completionists out there: just make sure the four guards are assassinated without using any weapons, and you should net the remaining 0.71%. Well done, you!

Edit: Added some historical context. One bag of rice back then had a purchasing power of about 700 to 1,000 USD today.

As an old fan of this series, I really hope Assassin's Creed can have a good future. I tried my best to understand this game and ignore some negative comments about Shadows, but there are some details that make me feel a little confused.

In the game, we can see these rice bags left everywhere carelessly. They are placed beside the roads, or even right in the middle of the roads. We can also see them in wide open spaces, and in the messy corners of bandit camps. There is no proper storage and no cover for them, so they just stay under the sun and the rain.

For Asian people, rice is not just food to fill our stomachs, but it is also a very important soul that connects our family emotions, our culture, and our history. Americans might not eat bread every day, and Italians might not eat pizza every day, but we really eat rice every single day.

Therefore, leaving these rice bags everywhere. And they have no cover, so they stay under the sun and rain, which makes the rice become useless garbage. Seeing rice bags randomly placed anywhere under the rain makes me feel a little sad.

More importantly, in the Japanese Sengoku period, "rice" was actually the salary for samurai. Their income was calculated by how much rice they received. Those are not ordinary sacks, but standardized rice bales called *kome-dawara*. They held a defined quantity of rice with clear economic value and were used for taxation, stipends, and trade. They usually contained brown rice. At the time, rice was a major tax resource, military supply, and the basis of samurai stipends. Leaving rice bales like that would expose important food and valuable property to moisture, fire, theft, or damage.

r/assassinscreed - According to the official Nagano Inavalley Tourism Bureau
According to the official Nagano Inavalley Tourism Bureau
For example, Yasuke’s master, Oda Nobunaga, his historical income was "7 million Koku", which is about 1 billion kilograms of white rice. If Nobunaga gave Yasuke his salary, it would also be rice.

I cannot help but wonder, does UBI maybe not know that those are bags for valuable food? Is it possible that the management gave the studio these texture assets, but the staff did not recognize what they were, so they just pasted them to fill the empty space?

Also, perhaps for the light and shadow system, there are too many lighting facilities, like many bonfires, torches, and lamp stands.

At that time, almost all buildings were made of wood, so this looks very dangerous. Torches are even placed right next to straw and rice bags.

Even if I try not to worry about these things, seeing lamps lighted outdoors in the broad daylight is still a bit strange for me. I really hope the development team can notice these small details.
label: analysis

When you hover over abbey locations on the map, the ambient chant that plays is actually "Chestneyshuyu Kheruvim" (More Honorable than the Cherubim) – a well-known Eastern Orthodox hymn sung in Church Slavonic. I recognized it because I'm Orthodox Christian and hear it regularly at services. The thing is, 9th century Anglo-Saxon England was entirely Latin rite. Church Slavonic liturgy would have had no place there historically. Looks like Ubisoft's sound team grabbed a sample from a library without checking which Christian tradition it belongs to. Prefer the command line? This auto-detects your language, no hex editor.

Run in the AC2 install folder. Makes a .bak, asserts the layout before writing, so it can't corrupt the file. (Linux/macOS/WSL, or any Python on Windows.)
python3 - <<'PY'
import re, shutil
f   = "uplay_install.state"
LOC = rb"[a-z]{2}-[A-Z]{2}"                 # de-DE, fr-FR, ru-RU, zh-CN, ...
d   = open(f, "rb").read()
assert len(re.findall(rb"\x1a\x05"     + LOC, d)) == 1, "head token not found"
assert len(re.findall(rb"\xd2\x01\x05" + LOC, d)) == 1, "tail token not found"
shutil.copy(f, f + ".bak")
d = re.sub(rb"(\x1a\x05)"     + LOC, rb"\1en-US", d, count=1)
d = re.sub(rb"(\xd2\x01\x05)" + LOC, rb"\1en-US", d, count=1)
open(f, "wb").write(d)
print("Done -> en-US (backup at %s.bak)" % f)
PY
For a different target language, replace both en-US with your code (e.g. fr-FR).

text:
The Origin of 'The Creed'

As you can likely guess, the Creed originates back to the days of Bayek of Siwa (38BC), when he and his wife, Aya, formed The Hidden Ones. However, it wasn't until the days of Altaïr Ibn-La'Ahad (1191AD) that we learned of the three tenants of 'The Creed'.

The Three Tenants of the Assassin's Creed

Stay your blade from the flesh of the innocent. - Originally introduced by Bayek of Siwa, this is put in place to avoid Assassins from deviating from their path as precise killers - only killing those who justly deserve it.

Hide in plain sight. - The Assassins aren't an order that wants to affect the world through guidance or manipulation, only remove those who seek to control the free-will of others. This also adds to the mysterious or supernatural effect of Assassins appearing from nowhere and seemingly disappearing just as easily.

Never compromise the Brotherhood. - A simple one of self preservation. If an assassin is ever being pursued, they must never directly retreat to a known assassin hideout. If an assassin is captured and questioned, they must never reveal any of the orders secrets.

I found a very simple solution for Assassin’s Creed 1 stuttering on PC (Windows 10/11).

Problem: The game stutters every few seconds even on decent hardware. Tried V-Sync off, affinity, FPS cap, etc. — nothing fully worked.

Solution (very simple): ➡️ Disconnect from the internet and play the game OFFLINE.

Steps:

Turn off Wi-Fi / unplug Ethernet.

Launch Assassin’s Creed 1.

Play normally.

Result: Stuttering disappears or is significantly reduced.

No mods. No config files. No extra programs.

Explanation (possible reason): The game tries to connect to old Ubisoft online services that no longer work, causing periodic freezes. Playing offline stops these checks.

The quests are this week's "Trials of the Gods." https://support.ubisoft.com/en-GB/Faqs/000032123/Trials-of-the-Gods-ACO/

Don't even go near them before you're level 38 at least. Unless you enjoy pain.

I don't recommend the level boost to new players. It was meant for returning players when the 2nd DLC "Curse of the Pharaohs" came out. Boosting yourself to 45 will dump a truckload of skill points on you, so you'll be unlocking almost your entire skill tree at once. That will most likely be overwhelming. It's better to unlock your skills one-by-one and find out what each one can do for you before getting the next.

You should learn which weapons are "best" by giving them all a try and finding out which class suits your playstyle. They all have pros and cons. Generally it's a good idea to have two very different ones equipped in the two slots, so that you can switch quickly as needed, i. e. some daggers for brawling and maybe a spear for when you're fighting mounted.

Clothing has no stats in Origins so you can choose any outfit you like.

Shields have resistance perks. Choose one with resistances that are appropriate to the task at hand. For example, when you're going to clear a crocodile lair you don't need ranged resistance on your shield because crocodiles are unlikely to shoot arrows at you. You want melee resistance in this case. When you find a shield that has resistances for both major damage types (melee and ranged), hold on to it. There is no shield in the game that has resistances to all three damage types (melee, ranged and fire) so it's always a trade-off.

text:
Skill issue.

Edit:

Genuinely if you're having problems with movement and parkour, that is a skill issue. Altair only does stuff if you press the buttons to make him do that, but he will do anything you push the buttons for, even if it means flinging himself off a roof or climbing something you didn't want to climb. Have better button discipline and be more mindful of which direction you're actually telling him to go.

If you're going around a corner, don't hold the legs button, slow down to the jog instead of the sprint to make sure you don't accidentally climb. You have 4 movement speeds for a reason, use them.

The NPCs aren't poorly designed, they're operating exactly as intended. The beggars have one of several repeating NPC dialogues that make up the background noise in the cities (like the town criers and merchant stalls). This is so that when you hear people talking about something other than the basic city dialogue, you know you're near an investigation opportunity. The game was originally designed to be played without a map or HUD, so it uses audio cues like that.

The jar carriers, beggars, and crazy people are intentional obstacles placed in the game to make you think and move more carefully. If there's a bunch of stuff at ground level getting in your way, go to the rooftops. Social stealth obstacles are easy to navigate around if you just pay attention.

If you think AC1 is the worst game you've ever played, you need to play more games.

The first game, hands-down, because it's the only game to be set in an era where the historical Assassins and Knights Templar actually existed, and most of the targets are based on real historical figures. With that said, there's still a lot of artistic license in the designs of the cities (there was definitely no giant Gothic cathedral in Acre in 1191), some historical figures, and of course the Apple of Eden is fictional... but overall, it's the one time where the central Assassins vs. Templars plot is pretty true to life.

The rest of the series skews quite well in historic accuracy, at least for certain events, but connecting events to the Assassins vs. Templars metaplot does mean they lose some points for historical accuracy. Disregarding that, I'd say that ACII does a good job with some of its historic events (the Pazzi conspiracy, the battle of Forli and the Bonfire of the Vanities especially) and ACIII gives a passable, albeit very abridged, look at the American Revolution.

text:
If you’re talking about AC1 with Altair then there’s a lot to cover. I’m far from the best AC1 player and there’s even more to the game, but these are some of the basic tips and tricks.

COMBAT: The original Assassin’s Creed and the Ezio Trilogy that follows it uses a ‘combo system’ for its combat system. This combo system works with you timing your strikes in a rhythm where you press the attack button just as your weapon hits the enemy. Repeat this and you’ll pull off a combo! Pulling these combos off will become really important in the later parts of the game as the enemies will get tougher. They’ll start to counter Altair’s attacks if you button mash/ spam attack and you’ll find yourself kissing the dirt a lot if you do spam. The tail end of the game has a ton of forced combat encounters so best you learn it.

People will say to just counter attack your way through all of the combat encounters for an easy time, but that’s a bit of lie (kinda) and I don’t recommend it. The only weapon that will guarantee a one hit counter kill every time is the hidden blade and it’s super high risk but high reward. Hidden blade counters require even more precise counter timing than the regular weapons and you can’t block with the hidden blade. This makes it even more risky in the earlier parts of the game where you’ll only have a few segments of health. Also overusing the counter attack is a great way to make the game as unfun as possible.

EXPLORATION: Do synch points to reveal the map. Doing so will reveal investigations and civilians in trouble. Completing as many of these missions is the only way to raise your health bar as far as I know. Rescuing civilians will also plant vigilantes around the city who will distract guards in your fights and escapes when in proximity. Also the game doesn’t tell you this very well but some of your investigations can give you things like a map of patrol routes. These can be accessed in a menu somewhere.

Oh and don’t bother with collecting the flags. They’re ultimately pointless and the devs put them in as a bit of troll for completionists.

PARKOUR: Altair is a slower climber than future protagonists. Use parkour starters to get onto rooftops fast. Also take advantage of side and back ejects when applicable to skip the slow climbing.

Don’t be afraid to release the sprint button if you want to go slower and have more control for things like turns. When you relearn the grasp ledge move, use it as much as possible as the game won’t always cling you to the nearest handhold. It’ll save you from some broken ankles and death.

Archers are littered across the rooftops and they might try to stop you while you’re parkouring. Just lock onto these pests and use a throwing knife to (always) take them out in one hit.

I’d recommend watching Leo K and Jcers’ videos on YouTube of AC1 so you can take full advantage of the game’s parkour system.

MODERN DAY: These sections may seem boring as at first glance as it appears to just be a walking simulator. However, as you progress through Altair’s memories, you’ll find out that you’re not as helpless as you may think. You may or may not be able to do some pickpocketing and exploration...

I played the first three games when they came out and I liked them, but after that, most of the titles always lost me after a couple of hours. The constant bugs didn’t help either (I’m looking at you, Black Flag, with NPCs disappearing right in front of me). Even the newer, more polished ones like Origins didn’t really click with me, even though I love how they look and how the maps are designed.

Then I realized what my real problem was: the amount of information on screen. There’s always something popping up: markers, icons, messages, objectives, distances, etc. It never lets you just be in the world.

So I decided to play using only the compass and nothing else. No minimap, no markers, no UI clutter. And honestly? The game became 100% better.

I got that feeling back of being lost, of actually exploring, of wondering “What’s over that hill?” instead of just following icons. It feels more immersive, more natural, and more like an actual adventure.

If you’re like me and the saga never really clicked with you, I highly recommend turning off the HUD and giving it another try.

Just to clarify: I almost never tweak game settings because I like experiencing the developer’s original vision. But please, Ubisoft… stop treating players like they’re dumb. This has been a criticism from the community for years.

This applied to the PS3/WiiU releases so unless they've changed some fundamentals this should apply to the remaster as well.

Don't buy weapons for the first playable character if you want to save money early on. They don't carry over and you don't really need them at that point. Don't be afraid to grab chests and collectibles though as they do carry over and you can find the money you collected as this character in a logically placed chest later.

Explore the city undergrounds early to unlock city fast travel points.

Liberate districts early to receive district keys so you don't have to lockpick district chests.

Grab chests, harvest valuable animals you come across, save your money and use trade convoys early and often to get a headstart moneywise. Clearing forts/naval missions also increases the revenue from trade/naval convoys.

Leveling up your homestead craftspeople nets you some nice ammo upgrades etc. so it's worth it to keep up with their missions as soon as available.

Pickpocket civilians whenever the opportunity rises to get crafting materials/delivery request items and to unlock the thieves challenge sets.(after starting sequence 5) Fancy clothing usually means higher value/more rare items.

Defeat an enemy using fists only after starting sequence 5 to grab the attention of the brawlers and beat “Boston's Most Wanted” to unlock brawler challenge sets.

After finishing sequence 4, visit a Frontiersmen campfire in the frontier to begin the first mission, “The Boy Who Cried Wolf” to open up challenge sets.
